finding: The marker §3 adopts for prospectivity does not discriminate: it was populated seven releases ago, so "the reset applies to rounds recorded from this release forward" is false for every audit round on disk. Measured: audit_record.go:213 stamps IDScheme: engine.IDSchemeSlug on every audit round it records, and reviewstate.go:44 dates that marker to v0.30.0+. All nine of v0.35.0's audit rounds carry "id_scheme": "slug" in spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json (lines 203, 213, 223, 233, 243, 253, 263, 273, 283), so engine.IsLegacyRound (reviewstate.go:503-505, r.IDScheme == "") returns FALSE for all nine. Under §3's rule -- "applies the reset only from the first marked round onward" -- every round of v0.29.0 onward is marked and the reset is retroactive across the whole corpus, which is exactly the outcome §3's own simulation says is unacceptable (blocking 3 -> 8, all 9 -> never). Test 10 therefore asserts a false expected value AND names its killing mutation backwards: it says "dropping the IsLegacyRound check ... makes v0.35.0's recorded history report all as never-converged", but KEEPING the check produces that result, because none of those rounds is legacy. Test 6 pins the contradiction inside the same release: it asserts all converges at round 9 on the same nine rounds. The two tests cannot both pass.
suggestion: IsLegacyRound answers "are this round's item ids comparable", not "was this round recorded before the reset shipped", and reusing it silently inherits a v0.30.0 boundary. Record a NEW marker at audit_record.go alongside IDScheme (a reset/round-schema stamp, or a tp version), define the boundary as "the first round carrying that stamp", and build test 10's fixture from rounds this release recorded plus older unstamped ones -- not from v0.35.0's history, which is stamped. Then test 6's replay is legal because the copied testdata carries no new stamp.

finding: Test 11 pins one command form and there are two write paths, so the test passes over an unfenced one -- and the unfenced one is the form tp's own shipped test already uses. Test 11: "tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1". It names no write target, and tp has two: the task override (set.go) and the project config (set_project.go, tp set --workflow --project). Measured: fenceWorkflowWrite (internal/cli/unattended.go:56) is reached from exactly four call sites -- set.go:414 and :428, set_project.go:98 and :108 -- all inside the float and integer branches. The string field this release is twinned on, review_converge_on, is handled at set.go:374-383 and hits `continue` before any fence call, so the twin structure §2 points at carries the bypass. An implementer satisfying test 11 on set.go alone leaves `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` exiting 0 under TP_UNATTENDED=1, and the test is green. §2 calls this fence "what the release buys"; the release's only test of it cannot tell the half-built fence from the built one. audit_signal_test.go:472 writes precisely the --project form.
suggestion: Give test 11 both targets and both directions: `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` and `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` each exit 2 with the escalation hint under TP_UNATTENDED=1, and each exit 0 without it. Say in §2 that widening the fence to string fields means widening it in set.go AND set_project.go, since fenceWorkflowWrite is today called only from their numeric branches.

finding: The call site added this round to close round 4's enumeration gap is cited in the wrong package, and the wrong file has a line 87 that looks plausible. §3: "Converged is reached from audit_record.go (twice), run_status.go, budget.go, **resume.go:87**". Measured: internal/cli/resume.go contains ZERO occurrences of the string `Converged`, and its line 87 is `return "", "", nil` inside resolveCycle's ReadTaskFile error branch. The real site is internal/**engine**/resume.go:87 -- `auditConverged := Converged(auditRounds, wf.AuditCleanRounds, specHash)`, with :86 computing reviewConverged from the same shared function. Every other bare filename in that paragraph (audit_record.go, run_status.go, budget.go, review_status.go:67, audit.go:352) resolves under internal/cli/, so a bare `resume.go:87` reads as internal/cli/resume.go:87 -- which exists, is plainly not a Converged call, and gives the implementer no signal that the package is different. The full production set of engine.Converged callers is five: audit_record.go:95, audit_record.go:333, review_status.go:67, run_status.go:149, budget.go:26, plus engine/resume.go:87.
suggestion: Write it as `engine/resume.go:86-87` and state the split: :86 (review) stays on Converged, :87 (audit) moves to ConvergedSince. While correcting it, note that the paragraph now spans two packages and mark which entries are cli/ and which engine/.

finding: §3 names the failure the resume site exists to prevent and §5 pins no test on it, so the release's most likely partial implementation passes all twelve tests. §3: omitting that site "leaves tp resume reporting phase: release on a streak the reset just invalidated, this section's own stated failure". No test in §5 mentions tp resume, DetectPhase or resumeblockers. Test 8's surface is `tp audit --status --check`, computed in internal/cli (audit_record.go / audit.go); phase: release is computed in internal/engine/resume.go:87 feeding engine.DetectPhase (phase.go:28-38) and engine.ResumeBlockers, a separate package with a separate call. The mutation "move the audit sites in internal/cli to the Since variants and leave engine/resume.go:87 on the shared Converged" is killed by nothing in the list: tests 8 and 9 both pass, test 12 passes, and tp resume still says release. That mutation is not hypothetical -- it is what §3's own round-4 enumeration would have produced, which is why the site was added this round.
suggestion: Add a test: on test 8's fixture (two clean rounds straddling a spec_hash boundary, last round's hash equal to the current spec), `tp resume` reports phase: audit rather than release. Assert the surface, not the function -- Non-Goal 4's protection of review's --status is asserted at a surface for the same reason.

finding: Test 9 now pins the expected value my round-4 finding asked for, but leaves the argument that decides it unstated, so the two engineers still write different assertions -- they just disagree by a different number. `ConsecutiveCleanSince(rounds []ReviewRound, current string) int` takes a second argument; test 9 gives the fixture ("rounds at hashes A, A, B") and the answer ("returns 1 -- the trailing run") and never says what `current` is. On that same fixture the function returns 1 if current == "B", and 0 if current == "A" or "" (the last round is at B, so the walk stops immediately). §3 defines `current` nowhere either: the table says only "stops at a spec_hash boundary", and the name `current` is the only hint that it is the current spec's hash. Test 8 is consistent with current == the last round's hash but never says so, and test 7 pins that equality as a property of a DIFFERENT fixture. So nothing in §5 states the parameter's meaning; "returns 1" is writable only by an engineer who guessed right.
suggestion: State in §3 that `current` is the current spec's hash (the same value Converged already receives), and give test 9 both readings as one assertion pair: on rounds A, A, B, ConsecutiveCleanSince(..., "B") == 1 and ConsecutiveCleanSince(..., "A") == 0, against ConsecutiveClean == 3. The second is the negative control that catches an implementation ignoring the argument.

finding: Tests 2-6 all ask whether a round is clean under a policy, and the release names no function or surface that computes that, while §3 names both of its additions by full signature. §2 states the predicate as prose and stops. The two functions §3 adds -- ConsecutiveCleanSince and ConvergedSince -- both take []ReviewRound whose Clean field is already set, and §2.2 says Clean is stamped at record time, so neither can apply audit_converge_on to anything. Something must map (a round's rows, a policy) -> clean, and it is unnamed. The review side has exactly that named twin set: engine.ReviewRoundClean(specPath, *ReviewRound, convergeOn) at internal/engine/reviewclean.go:56, plus ReviewConsecutiveClean (:119) and ReviewConverged (:134) documented there as the severity-aware mirrors of ConsecutiveClean and Converged. The audit release ships the Since pair and no audit twin of ReviewRoundClean. Test 6 is the sharpest case: replaying nine stored rounds under two policies requires re-deriving Clean from rows before ConsecutiveCleanSince can be called at all. Two engineers write a unit test against a new engine function, a CLI test against `tp audit --status`, and a CLI test against `tp audit --record`, and those three surfaces do not agree (--record stamps, --status could recompute).
suggestion: Name the audit twin in §3's table beside the two Since functions -- e.g. `engine.AuditRoundClean(specPath, *ReviewRound, convergeOn) bool`, mirroring reviewclean.go:56 -- and say for each of tests 2-6 whether it calls that function or a CLI surface. §2 already asserts the predicate; giving it a name is what makes tests 2-6 writable without inventing API.

finding: "The reversal is exactly two of its eleven assertions" is true as a count and false as a description of blast radius, and test 12 inherits the error. The eleven are confirmed: audit_signal_test.go:473, 474, 481, 484, 485, 490, 493, 494, 497, 498, 500. But :472-474 assert that `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` FAILS. Once the field ships, that command succeeds and WRITES audit_converge_on=blocking into the fixture's project config, so the nine remaining assertions execute under `blocking` rather than under the default -- a different policy from the one §4 says survives. They do survive, but only through a rule §4 never mentions: signalRow (audit_signal_test.go:40-42) emits `{item_id, role, status}` and no `severity` key at all, so the go-safety FAIL row has an ABSENT severity and §2's fail-closed rule counts it as blocking. Reverse §2's fail-closed rule and nine of eleven assertions in a test §4 promises is untouched go red. Two engineers implement the reversal differently: one flips :473-474 to expect exit 0 and leaves the write standing, one deletes the `set` call to keep the fixture at its default.
suggestion: Say which. If the write stands, add to §4 that the nine survive because the fixture's rows carry no severity and §2's fail-closed rule applies -- and note the consequence for test 12: it is then also a fail-closed test, so its failure is ambiguous with test 5(c) and cannot localise the defect. If the call is deleted, say so, because deleting it is a thirteenth edit to a file §4 says takes exactly two.

finding: Test 9's surface half names a line that does not read the fixture's stored flags, so "still reports 3" is not writable from the fixture test 9 describes. "Asserted on both the function and the surface: review_status.go:91's consecutive_clean still reports 3." Measured: internal/cli/review_status.go:63-65 overwrites every entry -- `rounds[i].Clean = engine.ReviewRoundClean(specPath, &rounds[i], wf.ReviewConvergeOn)` -- BEFORE line 91 calls engine.ConsecutiveClean, and its own comment says "never the stored boolean". engine.ReviewRoundClean (internal/engine/reviewclean.go:56-77) falls back to entry.Clean only when the round's file is missing (:57-60); when the file exists it recomputes from the rows under the resolved review_converge_on and the current resolution state. So a fixture of three rounds stamped `clean: true` in state.json reports 3 at :91 if the three round files are absent, and reports whatever the rows compute if they are present -- and my own round-4 finding asserted the opposite about this line, which is how the citation reached the spec. This also makes test 9 the only test whose answer moves when an unrelated setting (review_converge_on) is resolved differently.
suggestion: Pin the fixture: state whether the three review rounds have round files on disk, and if they do, that their rows are clean under the resolved review_converge_on. Simplest deterministic form: no round files, so ReviewRoundClean returns the stored flag verbatim and :91 reads 3 for the reason the test intends.

finding: §2 names the two surfaces whose omission cost a whole release last time, declares them in scope, and §5 pins no test on either. "v0.31.1 exists as a whole release because v0.31.0 shipped review_converge_on without `tp config --extract` and `validate --project`. Both are in this release's scope." Neither string occurs anywhere in §5. Test 1 covers resolution precedence and the invalid-value refusal, which is exactly the coverage v0.31.0 already had when it shipped the gap -- a resolver can be complete and correct while `tp config --extract` omits the field and `tp validate --project` neither accepts nor rejects it. So the release records the historical failure and ships without the guard against repeating it, in a list whose stated purpose is that four earlier drafts contained a test that passed against unmodified tp.
suggestion: Add a test: `tp config --extract` emits audit_converge_on with its resolved value, and `tp validate --project` accepts `all`/`blocking` and rejects a third value with the §2 hint. Its killing mutation is the v0.31.0 defect itself -- a field wired into the resolver and into neither reporting surface.

finding: §3's partition -- "The audit sites move to the Since variants; the review sites do not" -- is unwritable at one of the five sites it enumerates, because that site is neither. Measured: internal/cli/budget.go:21-36, refuseIfBudgetExhausted, computes `converged := engine.Converged(rounds, requiredClean, specHash)` at :26 for BOTH kinds and overwrites it at :28 only `if kind == "review"`. So :26 is one call serving audit and review, and the partition gives two different implementations: replace :26 outright with ConvergedSince (correct, because the review value at :26 is dead once :28 overwrites it, but it reads as changing a review site) or add a `kind == "audit"` branch (three branches where the file has two). §5 pins no test at that surface at all -- the exit-4 round-budget refusal -- so whichever is chosen ships unasserted, and the observable difference is real: under the reset, an audit sequence at its cap whose streak the boundary just invalidated must be refused where today it is let through.
suggestion: Say which form :26 takes, and add the assertion: at audit_max_rounds reached with a spec_hash boundary inside the trailing clean run, `tp audit --record` exits 4 with the budget message where the same fixture without the boundary exits 0.

finding: §5's preamble -- "Every test names the input that makes it fail" -- is false for two of the twelve, so the list is twelve items and ten assertions plus one fixture clause. Test 7 asserts nothing about tp: its content is a constraint on test 8's fixture ("This fixture's LAST round's spec_hash equals the current spec hash, so only §3's reset can move the answer") and its subject is stated as "so a naive fixture satisfies test 8". There is no input to test 7 and no observable to compare; an implementer producing an artifact called "test 7" produces either a duplicate of test 8 or a tautology. Test 12 names neither an input nor a mutation: "The nine surviving assertions of TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate still pass" is a statement about an existing file, and the release's edit to that file is the thing under test.
suggestion: Fold 7 into 8 as a fixture clause ("...with the last round's spec_hash equal to the current spec hash, so the pre-existing !StateStale term cannot supply the answer"), and give 12 its input -- run the test file, with the two reversed assertions rewritten and no other line changed, and assert the diff to that file touches only lines 473-474.

finding: Test 6 pins the fixture's content as "the `(status, severity)` pairs" of nine recorded rounds, which discards the two fields --record's clean determination is computed after. Non-Goal 2 states that dedupAuditRows keeps the first (role, item_id) row; a round's recorded findings count and clean flag are post-dedup, so from bare pairs a harness cannot reproduce either. On this particular corpus it happens not to matter -- measured, each of the nine audit-round-N.ndjson files holds exactly 200 rows with zero duplicate (role, item_id) keys, so dedup is a no-op and the pinned answers 3 and 9 stand -- but the fixture shape encodes that accident rather than the rule, and a later maintainer regenerating the testdata from a corpus that does contain duplicates gets different answers with no signal. Recorded here as a shape issue, not as a wrong number: rounds 1-9 carry 12, 12, 5, 4, 6, 1, 2, 0, 0 non-PASS rows with errors only in rounds 1 (2) and 4 (1), so blocking is clean from round 2 and converges at 3, and all converges at 9, both at audit_clean_rounds 2 -- test 6's arithmetic reproduces exactly, as do its at-1 answers of 2 and 8.
suggestion: Copy the rows whole rather than the pairs, or say the pairs are taken post-dedup from the recorded round file and that the test constructs ReviewRound entries directly instead of running --record over the testdata.

finding: Near-miss, and the defect it nearly hid is this round's critical. My round-4 finding asked §3 to name a stored discriminator for prospectivity and SUGGESTED engine.IsLegacyRound by name as the precedent to copy. §3 adopted it verbatim. Because the suggestion was mine I nearly took the repair as closed and moved on; the thing that stopped me was checking the marker's vintage rather than its shape. It is populated by audit_record.go:213 on every audit round and dates to v0.30.0 (reviewstate.go:44), so it marks seven releases of existing rounds as non-legacy and makes the reset retroactive -- the exact failure §3 quotes IsLegacyRound to prevent. The general form, and the reason it is worth a row: a reviewer's own suggestion arrives in the next draft already carrying the reviewer's authority, and the round that reads it is the round least likely to test it. A citation is a claim about the code even when the reviewer wrote it.
suggestion: No action on the spec beyond the critical filed at §3. For the loop: when a repair cites an artifact a previous round's SUGGESTION named, re-derive the artifact rather than the repair.

finding: Near-miss, caught by re-measuring with a second tool. faster_search {c: true} counts OCCURRENCES, not matching lines, and I read its output as a row count. It reported 202 hits for "severity" and 194 for "status":"PASS" in spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/audit-round-5.ndjson, from which I derived that the file held 202 rows and 8 non-PASS against the 6 that round recorded, and had begun drafting a critical that §1's "42 non-PASS rows" is really 44, that two rows carry no gradeable severity, and that §2.2's "zero out-of-enum severities across v0.33.0-v0.36.0" is therefore false. Parsing the file directly: 200 rows, 6 non-PASS, all warning, zero duplicate (role, item_id) keys -- two rows simply use the word "severity" inside notes. Re-derived over every audit-round-*.ndjson in the repository, §1 and §2 and §2.2 and test 4 are all exact: 42 non-PASS in v0.35.0 split 3 error / 22 warning / 17 info; 2,913 PASS rows across v0.35.0-v0.36.0 every one severity null; 238 non-PASS across v0.33.0-v0.36.0 with zero out-of-enum; 158 warning of 360 non-PASS corpus-wide; and all 67 out-of-enum rows (high 16, medium 15, low 36) confined to v0.29.0-v0.32.0. A counting tool's units are part of the measurement.
suggestion: No action. Recorded as the round asks. §1's, §2's, §2.2's and test 4's figures are confirmed correct and should not be re-challenged on a row count.
